cover.headline: A capable machinist that has become a capital-hungry aluminium caster; the price assumes more than the numbers show
cover.lead: Craftsman Automation machines engine blocks and heads for trucks, tractors and gensets, casts and machines aluminium parts for car and two-wheeler makers, and builds storage and material-handling systems. Revenue grew 5.2x in five years to ₹8,069 cr (FY26), mostly in aluminium and partly through acquisitions; the EBITDA margin halved to 15%. Q1FY27 was strong (revenue +36%, PAT +116%) and a ₹2,000 cr QIP in Jun-2026 cut net debt to ~₹1,430 cr. We forecast EPS of ₹238 / ₹298 / ₹375 for FY27-29E on the post-QIP share count, below the street's ~₹350 for FY28E, because depreciation and interest absorb much of the EBITDA growth. The street values Craftsman on **P/E on FY28E EPS** (Motilal Oswal 28x; Emkay uses 17x EV/EBITDA). The house multiple, its 28.0x forward-P/E median since Apr-2021 cut by the 8.8% auto-component de-rating, is **25.5x Sep-28E EPS of ₹337 = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with SELL.** Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹5,707, DCF ₹4,454. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: A real engineering base, and a growth engine in aluminium
arguments.p: 35+ years of machining cylinder blocks and heads, in-house special-purpose machines, 31 plants, and a place in the supply chains of Indian and global engine makers. Aluminium revenue grew from ₹330 cr (FY21) to ₹4,789 cr (FY26); large-engine castings for data-centre gensets (US$100 mn a year by FY30, orders from 4-5 of 6 customers) and an industrial upcycle add new legs.

arguments.h: But the growth has cost a lot of capital and margin
arguments.p: Capex of ₹2,800 cr and ~₹800 cr of acquisitions in FY24-26, two QIPs (₹3,200 cr) in two years, borrowings up to ₹3,623 cr, EBITDA margin 28% → 15%, ROCE ~20% → 12-14% (Screener). Sunbeam, bought in Oct-2024, still earned single-digit EBITDA margins in FY26. One customer was 24% of standalone revenue.

arguments.h: Q1FY27 was good, and we model it
arguments.p: Revenue +36%, EBITDA margin 15.8%, PAT +116%. We model revenue +{{F.salesGrowth.0|n1}}% in FY27E, then +16% and +15%, and an EBITDA margin rising from {{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} to {{F.ebitdaMargin.2|pct}} as Sunbeam recovers. But capex of ₹1,500 cr in FY27 lifts depreciation and keeps net debt near ₹2,200-2,500 cr: our FY28E EPS (₹298) is ~14% below the street's, and ROE only reaches ~{{F.roe.2|pct}} by FY29E.

arguments.h: Valuation: the stock trades well above its own history
arguments.p: At ₹10,417 Craftsman trades at 31.0x our Sep-28E EPS and 58.6x trailing earnings, against a 28.0x forward-P/E median since Apr-2021, while auto-component peers trade 8.8% below their five-year medians. Even the street's post-Q1 targets (₹9,699-11,900) would mean 32.5-39.9x our FY28E EPS. We would turn HOLD only below ~₹9,030.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): whether aluminium pass-through and Sunbeam's exits lift the margin, and the first half-year balance sheet after the QIP (net debt, working capital).
The board's capex decision for FY27-28 (management said it would decide in Q3/Q4 whether to raise the ~₹1,500 cr plan).
Sale of Sunbeam's Gurgaon land ("close to signing a deal", Jul-2026): ~₹400 cr of debt reduction implied by the CMD.
Large-engine castings: approval of the cast parts (about a year) and first volume supplies in FY28.
Merger of DR Axion, Suprash and Srikara into Sunbeam (scheme filed); commissioning of DR Axion's Sriperumbudur plant (by Dec-2026).

sections.title: A contract manufacturer of machined metal parts: engine blocks, aluminium castings and storage systems

blocks.p: Craftsman Automation was founded in Coimbatore in 1986 by Srinivasan Ravi, who still runs it. It makes parts to its customers' drawings ("build to print"): it casts, machines, treats and assembles, but does not own the end product. It reports three segments. **Powertrain** (27% of FY26 revenue) machines cylinder blocks and heads, camshafts, transmission parts, bearing caps and turbocharger parts for truck, tractor, off-highway and stationary-engine makers, and since Oct-2024 casts large-engine parts in Germany (Craftsman Fronberg Guss). **Aluminium products** (59%) die-casts and machines engine, transmission and structural parts, EV battery housings and alloy wheels for car and two-wheeler makers, through Craftsman's own plants, DR Axion India and Sunbeam Lightweighting. **Industrial & engineering** (14%) makes storage solutions (racking, shelving, vertical and automated storage), material-handling equipment, gears and gearboxes, special-purpose machines and moulds, and does contract manufacturing.

sections.title: From a Coimbatore machine shop to a ₹8,000 cr group: three acquisitions and two QIPs in three years

blocks.p: For its first 30 years Craftsman was a powertrain machining company (blocks and heads for trucks and tractors) with a storage and engineering arm. It started aluminium die-casting in the 2000s and listed in Mar-2021. Since then it has bought its way into scale in aluminium: 76% of DR Axion India in Feb-2023 (a maker of critical aluminium castings for car makers), the rest in Jun-2024; Sunbeam Lightweighting (a loss-making die-caster with plants in the NCR) in Oct-2024; and the assets of a German iron foundry for large-engine castings in Oct-2024. Two QIPs (₹1,200 cr in Jun-2024 at ₹4,400; ₹2,000 cr in Jun-2026 at ₹8,700) paid for part of it. The founder sold 2% in Jun-2026, five days after the second QIP.

sections.title: Outsourcing, aluminium lightweighting and an industrial upcycle help; labour and capex costs are the squeeze

blocks.p: Craftsman's end markets moved in different directions in FY26-Q1FY27. Indian PVs and 2Ws grew and their makers are building greenfield plants and asking suppliers to follow (CMD: customers announcing 1,500-acre, ₹3,000-20,000 cr sites). Tractors did better; trucks were 'somewhat muted' (Q4 call). Industrial demand turned up: material-handling and storage orders rose quarter on quarter ('the capex cycle started in India', Q1 call). Data-centre and gas-genset demand created a new market for large-engine castings, with global suppliers 'full' on capacity (Q4 call).

bullets: **Aluminium.** Aluminium die-casting is fragmented and capital-hungry; global leaders are US$3-6 bn companies and several Indian listed peers from the north and west have plants near Chennai. Customers increasingly want casting plus machining in one place; raw castings 'are not going to be viable' as aluminium, energy, labour and consumables costs rise (CMD, Q4 call). Aluminium is passed through, but with a lag, and some customers 'take their own time' (Q1 call).

**Outsourcing.** Engine-block and head machining is being outsourced by OEMs that used to do it in-house, and global engine makers are moving supply to India ('China plus one'); Craftsman has been doing this since the 1990s and built in-house special-purpose machines to keep costs down.

**Costs.** Labour is the cost management worries about most: minimum wages are being reset and the new labour codes (notified 21-Nov-2025) raise costs; the CMD expects manpower inflation of ~20% a year in places and says it is 'very difficult to pass on'. Replacement capex costs 5-7x what the same capacity cost in 2016 (land 8-9x, construction 3-4x, machines ~2x in rupees), which raises the entry barrier but also Craftsman's own reinvestment bill.

**Electrification.** Most of Craftsman's powertrain revenue depends on diesel engines (trucks, tractors, gensets). EVs need no cylinder block or head; Craftsman's EV exposure is aluminium (battery housings, cooling trays, motor housings) and is small. Trucks, tractors and gensets will electrify much later than cars, which buys time.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** Craftsman sells capacity and know-how, not products. Its growth comes from customers outsourcing more and building new plants nearby, so it must invest ahead of orders. That makes volumes and margins depend on utilisation: ~70% in powertrain, >80% in aluminium, ~10% on the new large-engine lines (management, Jul-2026).

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** the tailwinds reach Craftsman's revenue, which is why it has grown ~39% a year since FY21. They have reached its returns much less: the fastest-growing segment earns the lowest margin, and every leg of growth (aluminium plants, large-engine foundry, new campuses) has required capital first and profit later.

sections.title: Powertrain: the high-margin core, back to growth, with large-engine castings from FY28

blocks.p: Powertrain is where Craftsman made its name: machining cylinder blocks and heads, camshafts and transmission parts for engine makers that outsource them. Machining an engine block takes dedicated lines, tight tolerances and years of approvals; Craftsman builds many of its own special-purpose machines, which keeps capital costs down, and says it was "instrumental in import substitution" for critical parts. Revenue grew from ₹811 cr (FY21) to ₹2,179 cr (FY26), but the margin has swung: 25-27% EBIT in FY21-23, 19% in FY24, 14% in FY25 (four to five quarters of heavy repair and maintenance, per the CMD) and back to 17% in FY26 and 18% in Q1FY27 (newer products at newer prices, manpower savings). Utilisation is ~70% against an optimum of 75-80%.

blocks.p: **Large engines.** Since 2021 Craftsman has been preparing to cast and machine crankcases and heads for large stationary engines (gensets for data centres, gas engines). It bought a German foundry (Fronberg Guss) in 2024 and built a foundry at Kothavadi. Large stationary-engine (data-centre gensets) castings and machining: US$100 mn a year by FY30 from 6 customers (orders from 4-5 received); ~30% of that run-rate productionised in FY28, ~50% in FY29; revenue 'very low single digit' share of powertrain in FY27 (Q4 and Q1 calls). The CMD says start-up costs are already in the numbers and return ratios on the new business should match the current powertrain "within a couple of years"; until then low utilisation will depress EBIT on that portion.

blocks.callout: **So what:** powertrain earns the group's best margins and is not capital-starved. Large-engine castings are a genuine new market (customers took ~4 years to approve Craftsman, so competitors cannot copy it quickly), but at US$100 mn a year by FY30 they add ~₹950 cr of revenue to a group of ₹10,000 cr: helpful, not transformational, and concentrated in six customers.

sections.title: Aluminium: 61% of FY27E revenue, ~10% EBIT, and the reason capex never stops

blocks.p: Aluminium is now Craftsman's largest business: ₹4,789 cr of revenue in FY26 (+58%) and 94,904 tonnes. It has three parts: Craftsman's own die-casting and machining (engine and transmission housings, structural parts, alloy wheels from Bhiwadi and Shoolagiri: ~₹280 cr of wheel revenue in FY26, an exit rate of ~3 million wheels a year against 5.8 million of capacity), DR Axion India (critical castings for car makers; a new 50-acre plant at Sriperumbudur from Dec-2026) and Sunbeam Lightweighting (bought in Oct-2024; mostly casting with little machining; being restructured). The plan is to merge DR Axion into Sunbeam and run the aluminium businesses together, with a first goal of US$1 bn of aluminium revenue in 2-3 years.

blocks.p: **Sunbeam.** Sunbeam came with ₹1,237 cr of annual revenue and a ₹232 cr pre-tax loss (FY25 pro forma, AR). Craftsman is exiting legacy parts and small customers, resetting prices and cutting staff, and sold a ~₹30 cr-a-year low-value line. Restructuring 90% complete by Dec-2026; exits loss-making legacy parts and customers (revenue may fall 10-20%); EBITDA margin 'mid-teens' by Q4FY27, in line with Craftsman (Q1 call, 30-Jul-2026). Was 'still at single-digit' in FY26 (Q4 call). If Sunbeam reaches a mid-teens EBITDA margin on ~₹1,000-1,100 cr of revenue, it adds roughly ₹100 cr of EBITDA to FY26's level; we assume part of that in the aluminium EBIT margin (10.3% in FY26 to 11.8% by FY29E).

blocks.callout: **So what:** aluminium gives Craftsman scale and growth but not returns: EBIT of ~10% on segment assets of ₹4,796 cr is a ~10% pre-tax return, below a 13% cost of equity. Management itself says margins will not rise 100-200bp while it keeps adding capacity at today's pace ("the future capex in this year will again spoil the margins"). The segment is where the bull and the bear cases are decided.

sections.title: Industrial & engineering: storage and material handling turned up in Q1FY27

blocks.p: The smallest segment (₹1,102 cr in FY26, 14% of revenue) is two businesses: storage solutions (~64% of FY26 segment revenue: racking, shelving, vertical stores, automated storage and retrieval systems, from Coimbatore, Bangalore and Pune) and engineering (special-purpose machines, material handling, gears and gearboxes, toolroom, sheet metal, contract manufacturing). The engineering arm also builds machines for Craftsman's own plants. EBIT margins collapsed from 19% (FY21) to 2% (FY25) and 4% (FY26) and jumped to 9% in Q1FY27 on operating leverage as material-handling and storage orders rose; the CMD says it is "not a one spike".

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Craftsman has a narrow moat in what it does best: machining complex iron parts for engine makers, with its own machines and decades of approvals. That moat does not extend to aluminium casting, where it competes with many Indian and global die-casters, customers control prices and returns are below the cost of capital. A good operator in a commoditising business is worth a fair multiple, not a premium one.

sections.title: Revenue up 5.2x in five years, mostly in aluminium; the EBITDA margin halved from 28% to 15%

blocks.p: Craftsman's consolidated revenue rose from ₹1,560 cr in FY21 to ₹8,069 cr in FY26 (Screener basis): 39% a year. Three things drove it. First, the aluminium business, ₹330 cr in FY21, became ₹4,789 cr in FY26 (59% of revenue) through new plants (alloy wheels at Bhiwadi and Shoolagiri) and two acquisitions: DR Axion (from Feb-2023) and the loss-making Sunbeam Lightweighting (from Oct-2024). Second, powertrain machining for trucks, tractors and off-highway engines grew from ₹811 cr to ₹2,179 cr. Third, industrial and engineering (storage, material handling, gears) grew from ₹419 cr to ₹1,102 cr. The EBITDA margin fell from 28% (FY21) to 15% (FY25-26) because aluminium earns far less than powertrain machining, Sunbeam lost money and new plants started half-empty. Net profit rose from ₹97 cr to ₹384 cr, but two QIPs (Jun-2024, Jun-2026) raised the share count by 24%, so EPS on today's 2.615 cr shares is ₹146.8 for FY26 (₹161 reported on the shares then outstanding).

blocks.callout: **Our view:** Craftsman is a growth company, but much of its growth is in a lower-quality business. Powertrain machining (17% EBIT margin in FY26) built the company; aluminium (10%) is now six-tenths of it, needs a new plant every year or two and passes metal prices through with a lag. Q1FY27 (revenue +36%, EBITDA margin 15.8%) shows the margin has stopped falling. Whether it can rise depends on Sunbeam reaching mid-teens EBITDA and new plants filling up, while the company keeps spending ₹1,000-1,500 cr a year.

bullets: **A beat.** Revenue was 9% above Emkay's estimate and 12% above the street's (Emkay, 31-Jul-2026); PAT doubled on a weak Q1FY26 base (₹8 cr exceptional charge, early Sunbeam).
**Aluminium** grew 38%: capacity is still being added and "some capacities are still not matured" (CMD); new orders start in FY28-29. Part of the growth is metal-price inflation passed through.
**Powertrain** grew 26%, which the CMD called a return to "a normal situation" after a muted period rather than a strong trend.
**Industrial & engineering** grew 53% with a 9% EBIT margin on material-handling and storage demand.
**Sunbeam** is 90% restructured by Dec-2026; mid-teens EBITDA margin targeted by Q4FY27.

sections.title: ₹2,800 cr of capex and ~₹800 cr of acquisitions in three years, funded by debt and two QIPs; returns are mediocre

blocks.p: Craftsman spends heavily: capex of ₹2,811 cr in FY24-26 (₹631 cr, ₹992 cr and ₹1,188 cr, 14-17% of revenue) against ₹657 cr in FY21-23. Cash from operations, ₹1,318 cr over the three years, covered less than half of it, because working capital absorbed ~₹1,200 cr as the aluminium business grew. Acquisitions (DR Axion's last 24%, Sunbeam, the German foundry, the Sriperumbudur land companies) took another ~₹794 cr. The gap was filled with ₹2,187 cr of net new borrowing and the ₹1,200 cr QIP of Jun-2024; the ₹2,000 cr QIP of Jun-2026 resets leverage again. ROCE on Screener's basis was 18-21% in FY22-24 and 12-14% in FY25-26; the company reports 16% for FY26 on average capital employed.

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** management argues that building plants early is cheaper than building them later (replacement cost 5-7x 2016 levels) and that operating leverage will come as plants fill. That may be true, but the record so far is that each new rupee of capital has earned less than the old ones: ROCE fell from ~20% to ~14% while capital employed tripled, and shareholders were asked for ₹3,200 cr in two years. Our model has ROE reaching only ~{{F.roe.2|pct}} by FY29E.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean audit, good cash conversion before capex; the issues are capital intensity and disclosure

bullets: **Cash conversion before capex is good.** Cash from operations (before interest, as Indian accounts show it) was 145% of net profit in FY25 and 136% in FY26 (₹522 cr), even after working capital absorbed ₹428 cr and ₹598 cr. Free cash flow after capex was ₹-706 cr and ₹-647 cr: negative for two years.

**Other income has one-offs.** FY26 other income of ₹61 cr (AR) included a ₹14.3 cr gain on asset sales and a ₹27.4 cr forex gain as the rupee fell; only ~₹20 cr is recurring. Exceptional charges were ₹25.5 cr (FY25) and ₹13.0 cr (FY26). Our FY27E other income of ₹{{F.otherIncome.0|num}} cr leans on interest on the QIP cash (Q1FY27 ₹24 cr; four quarters to Jun-26 ₹76 cr).
**Minorities:** until Jun-2024 Screener's Net Profit row included DR Axion's 24% minority; we use attributable profit ("Profit for EPS"), so FY24 profit is ₹304 cr, not ₹337 cr.

**Capitalisation:** the auditors list capitalisation of property, plant and equipment as a key audit matter. With ₹1,000-1,500 cr of capex a year, what is capitalised versus expensed (trial runs, pre-operative costs, borrowing costs) moves profit; disclosure is standard, not detailed.
**Disclosure:** segment EBIT and segment assets are reported, but not segment depreciation, entity results (Sunbeam, DR Axion), an order book or volumes outside aluminium tonnes.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** Unmodified audit opinion (Sharp & Tannan), modest exceptional items, cash conversion before capex above 100%. The weakness is economic, not accounting: the business needs a lot of capital, and free cash flow has been negative for two years.

sections.title: Net debt ~₹1,430 cr pro forma for the QIP; working capital and capex keep it from falling fast

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 Craftsman had ₹3,623 cr of borrowings on Screener's basis (long-term ₹2,411 cr, short-term ₹930 cr, leases ₹283 cr) against ₹193 cr of cash and investments: net debt ₹3,430 cr (the company reports ~₹3,100 cr and 2.43x EBITDA, excluding leases). The ₹2,000 cr QIP of 18-Jun-2026 brings pro forma net debt to ~₹1,430 cr, ~1.2x FY26 EBITDA; we add the QIP to the Mar-26 balance sheet in our model (net worth ₹5,264 cr pro forma vs ₹3,264 cr reported). Management says net debt / EBITDA will fall below 2x in FY27 and then towards 1.5x, and that it will not need to raise equity again. With ₹1,500 cr of capex and growing working capital, our model has net debt rising to ~₹2,250 cr by Mar-27 (1.4x EBITDA) and staying near that level. The Gurgaon land of Sunbeam, held for sale, could bring in ~₹400 cr (implied by the CMD); we do not count it.

sections.title: Governance: a capable founder-CEO, a small board and generous pay

blocks.p: Srinivasan Ravi, founder, Chairman & MD (mechanical engineer, PSG College of Technology; ~40 years in the industry). Ravi Gauthamram, Whole Time Director (promoter group; MS Production Systems Engineering, RWTH Aachen); on the board since Feb-2014. C.B. Chandrasekar (CFO); COO Thiyagaraj Damodharaswamy; CS Shainshad Aduvanni. Six directors: two executive promoters and four independent directors (Sundararaman Kalyanaraman, Vijaya Sampath, T.S.V. On Emkay's EPS (Sep-28E ₹385.8) our 25.5x would give ~₹9,840: still below the share price.

sections.title: The street after Q1: one Buy (EV/EBITDA), one Neutral (P/E); the stock ran past the Neutral target

blocks.p: Two notes after the Q1FY27 results were visible to us. **Emkay** (Buy, 31-Jul-2026) raised its target 14% to ₹11,900 at 17x Jun-28E EV/EBITDA (from 15x), arguing that Craftsman is "entering a strong growth phase" as large-engine castings, Sunbeam's turnaround and new aluminium capacity pay off. **Motilal Oswal** (Neutral since 2024) moved to ₹9,699 at 28x FY28E EPS, saying the run-up already prices in the strong delivery. Both forecast FY28E EPS of ~₹347-349. Median of the two targets: ₹10,800, +4% vs the 30-Sep-2026 close of ₹10,417. An S&P consensus of eight analysts showed an average target of ₹11,371 (31-Jul-2026). The stock rose from ~₹10,050 on results day to ₹10,417.

Growth has been bought as much as built: DR Axion (76% in Feb-2023, the last 24% for ₹250 cr in Jun-2024), Sunbeam (₹606 cr, loss-making) and the German foundry took aluminium from 21% of revenue (FY21) to 59% (FY26) and diluted the EBITDA margin from 28% to 15%.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a good machinist in a capital-hungry business, priced at 31x Sep-28E EPS; SELL

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** a founder-run engineering group with real machining know-how, 31 plants, a growing aluminium business (~95,000 tonnes), a new large-engine castings line with orders from global customers, and an industrial arm that is turning up. Revenue has grown ~39% a year since FY21, Q1FY27 was strong and the Jun-2026 QIP has repaired the balance sheet.

**What you are paying:** 43.8x our FY27E and 35.0x FY28E EPS for a business with a ~16% EBITDA margin, ROE of 11-14% in our forecasts and negative free cash flow in FY25-27E. That is well above the stock's own 28.0x forward-P/E median since listing, at a time when auto-component peers trade ~9% below theirs. On the street's method and the house multiple the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): SELL. Even our bull case ({{scen.bull.tp|inr}}) is only {{scen.bull.upside|chg}} above the price.

**The gap is mostly the multiple, partly earnings.** The stock trades at 31.0x our Sep-28E EPS against a house multiple of 25.5x (28.0x median × 0.912). Our FY28E EPS is ~14% below the street's; on Emkay's EPS our multiple would still give less than the share price. The post-Q1 street median target was ₹10,800.

rows: The main cast body of an engine (block) and the part bolted on top that holds the valves (head); both must be machined to tight tolerances.
Cutting a cast or forged part to its final shape and size on lathes, milling and boring machines.

Pouring or injecting molten metal into a mould; high-pressure (HPDC) for thin, complex aluminium parts, low-pressure (LPDC) for wheels and structural parts, gravity and sand casting for heavier parts.
Making a part to the customer's design: the supplier sells process skill and capacity, not its own product.
A machine built for one job or part, often by Craftsman itself.
Big diesel and gas engines for generator sets (e.g. data-centre back-up power) and industrial use.
Segment profit before corporate costs, other income, interest and tax, as the company reports it.
Qualified institutional placement: a share sale to institutions (₹1,200 cr in Jun-2024, ₹2,000 cr in Jun-2026).
Optionally convertible debenture: how Craftsman paid for and funded Sunbeam.
Restated as if an event (here, the Jun-2026 QIP) had already happened at Mar-2026.
Borrowings less cash, divided by a year's EBITDA: how many years of operating profit would repay the debt.
Share price ÷ earnings per share; enterprise value (market value plus net debt) ÷ EBITDA.
Half of FY28E plus half of FY29E: the 12-month-forward earnings the market will look at in September 2027.
How far comparable stocks trade below their own five-year median P/E on the valuation date.
Discounted cash flow valuation; WACC is the required annual return used to discount future cash (here the cost of equity).
